title: Sliding window
summary: Grow and shrink a contiguous window while updating a running answer.

parts.rule: Maintain a contiguous subarray or substring [left, right] while right advances over the input. Grow by including a[right]; shrink from the left when a constraint breaks. Update the answer from window state in constant or alphabet time per move so total time stays linear in n.
parts.why: Subarray problems look like quadratic nested loops. A window reuses work across adjacent intervals. Failures include shrinking too late, forgetting to update the running count when left moves, and applying a window to requirements that are not contiguous.
parts.example: Longest substring with at most two distinct characters on "eceba". Right moves across e, c, e, b, a while a count map tracks frequencies. After reading "ece" the map has e:2 and c:1 — still two keys, best length 3. Include b → three keys; advance left past the first e and then c until only two keys remain, leaving window "eb". Include a and shrink again. Best length stays 3. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so work is linear. For sum-at-most budget on [1, 2, 3, 4] with limit 5: grow until the sum exceeds five, shrink left, and track max length — legal windows include [1, 2] and [2, 3].
parts.use: Use a sliding window for longest or shortest subarray under a count or sum constraint, for fixed-length anagram scans, and for minimum-window cover when the feasibility constraint is monotone in window size. Use a deque of indices when you also need the window maximum in linear time.
parts.refuse: Refuse a window when the needed subset is not contiguous. Refuse claiming linear time if each shrink rescans the whole window from scratch. Refuse a fixed-size template for a variable-size constraint without the shrink loop. Refuse applying window logic to trees or graphs without first linearizing the input.

body:
Rule. Maintain a contiguous subarray or substring [left, right] while right advances over the input. Grow by including a[right]; shrink from the left when a constraint breaks. Update the answer from window state in constant or alphabet time per move so total time stays linear in n.

Why it matters. Subarray problems look like quadratic nested loops. A window reuses work across adjacent intervals. Failures include shrinking too late, forgetting to update the running count when left moves, and applying a window to requirements that are not contiguous.

Worked example. Longest substring with at most two distinct characters on "eceba". Right moves across e, c, e, b, a while a count map tracks frequencies. After reading "ece" the map has e:2 and c:1 — still two keys, best length 3. Include b → three keys; advance left past the first e and then c until only two keys remain, leaving window "eb". Include a and shrink again. Best length stays 3. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so work is linear. For sum-at-most budget on [1, 2, 3, 4] with limit 5: grow until the sum exceeds five, shrink left, and track max length — legal windows include [1, 2] and [2, 3].

When to use. Use a sliding window for longest or shortest subarray under a count or sum constraint, for fixed-length anagram scans, and for minimum-window cover when the feasibility constraint is monotone in window size. Use a deque of indices when you also need the window maximum in linear time.

When to refuse. Refuse a window when the needed subset is not contiguous. Refuse claiming linear time if each shrink rescans the whole window from scratch. Refuse a fixed-size template for a variable-size constraint without the shrink loop. Refuse applying window logic to trees or graphs without first linearizing the input.
